episodes.212265: Pulses in the southwesterly flow aloft once again encouraged thunderstorm development over portions of west Texas. One storm managed to produce a landspout near Fluvanna and half dollar-sized hail in Snyder.
episodes.212273: A shortwave in the southwesterly flow aloft allowed thunderstorms to develop during the afternoon of the 23rd. Storms developed first off the higher terrain and spread northeastward into the Permian Basin of west Texas. A few storms managed to produce large hail, along with some flash flooding.
episodes.212502: Showers and thunderstorms developed in a warm and humid airmass ahead of a cold front. Some storms produced heavy rainfall, leading to flooding.
episodes.212653: Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
episodes.212672: Marine Thunderstorms produced strong winds across the bays and gulf waters. A waterspout was also sighted as well.
episodes.212793: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts.  Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
episodes.212892: A warm front was lifted into the area by a passing low on the 23rd of May, then the front stalled over central West Virginia and southwest Virginia through the 24th. Another low eventually pushed the boundary northward and then steered a cold front west to east across the area on the 25th.||Rounds of rain and thunderstorms traversed southeast Ohio, with most robust activity occurring  in the afternoon and evening hours of the 23rd and 24th. Much of southeast Ohio received one to two and a half inches of rain during this time, along with pockets of three to four and a half inch accumulations. Excessive rainfall flooded roads in Athens, Jackson, Perry, Morgan, Gallia, Meigs, and Lawrence counties and led to minor flooding on portions of Sunday Creek, Duck Creek, and the Little Muskingum.
episodes.212902: A very moist and unstable air mass was in place across South Texas, with surface dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s and strong daytime heating producing moderate to strong instability. Sea-breeze boundaries along the Middle Texas Coast served as a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon. While upper-level winds were relatively weak, sufficient instability and moderate deep-layer shear supported organized convection capable of producing damaging wind gusts. A compact MCS developed near Corpus Christi and moved along the coast, where a favorable thermodynamic environment allowed it to intensify. The storm complex produced severe wind gusts, including measured gusts of 53-59 kt in Corpus Christi.
episodes.212907: A very moist and unstable air mass was in place across South Texas, with surface dewpoints in the lower to middle 70s and strong daytime heating producing moderate to strong instability. Sea-breeze boundaries along the Middle Texas Coast served as a focus for thunderstorm development during the afternoon. episodes.213023: A stalled frontal boundary north of the region, as well as Gulf Coast and Atlantic Coast sea breezes, combined with usual early summer high instability and PWATs close to 2 inches to produce numerous showers and thunderstorms across the region, as well as isolated severe downbursts. Slow storm motion attributed to localized heavy rainfall and minor flooding.
episodes.213029: A lingering stalled front remained in the forecast area 5/23, but a embedded shortwave in the general troughing pattern moved in during the afternoon and evening hours, leading to scattered convection to develop. The environment ahead of this shortwave was characterized by MLCAPE values over 2000 J/kg and effective shear near 30-35 kts. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across the forecast area during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing damaging winds, and hail up to golf ball sized.
episodes.213030: A lingering stalled front remained in the forecast area 5/23, but a embedded shortwave in the general troughing pattern moved in during the afternoon and evening hours, leading to scattered convection to develop. The environment ahead of this shortwave was characterized by MLCAPE values over 2000 J/kg and effective shear near 30-35 kts. Scattered strong to severe storms moved across the forecast area during the afternoon and evening hours, bringing damaging winds, hail up to golf ball sized, and even a report of a waterspout over Lake Murray in SC.
episodes.213210: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed on a daily basis across the region over Memorial Day weekend as a result of several passing upper level disturbances. Some storms produced severe hail, damaging winds, and flash flooding. Significant flash flooding occurred in North Richland Hills in Tarrant County on May 25th.
episodes.213310: A diffuse frontal boundary stalled across the northern forecast area 5/22 with broad troughing present. Areas south of the boundary saw generous heating with MLCAPE values nearing 1500-2000 J/kg and weak deep layer shear near 25-30 kts. This heating across the boundary lead to a couple strong storms, but one that produced tree damage near Thomson GA and started a fire at McCormick High School in McCormick County SC.
episodes.213317: Severe thunderstorms occurred across the Texas Panhandle from during the late afternoon through late evening hours on May 22nd through May 24th. On the 22nd the environment was such that a few isolated storms were able to produce hail between one inch and 2.75 inches across parts of the southern Texas Panhandle. On the 23rd, thunderstorms produced straight line winds in excess of 58 mph across the central to northern Texas Panhandle. Additional severe wind gusts also occurred on the 24th. Several landspouts also occurred during this time period. An additional landspout also occurred on May 26th in the southwest Texas Panhandle.
episodes.213329: A slow moving low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley region, bringing rounds of heavy rainfall.
episodes.213371: A slowly decaying line of thunderstorms across western-north Texas produced strong winds and small hail during the very late evening of the 22nd.
episodes.213372: A supercell thunderstorm developed in far northern Roger Mills County on the evening of the 23rd, producing a report of large hail before quickly dissipating.
episodes.213406: An upper level low pressure system was situated over the Northern Plains during the early morning hours of May 23 with an associated shortwave trough over the central CONUS. As the morning progressed into the afternoon, the shortwave trough continued to push east toward the Missouri Ozarks. Instability increased ahead of the trough, near a remnant Mesoscale Convective Vortex, and near a stationary front across central Missouri. Scattered slow-moving thunderstorms developed across portions of Kansas into Missouri as a result, with heavy rainfall leading to flooded roads across portions of Barry, Dallas, and Jasper counties.
episodes.213470: A cluster of thunderstorms formed over southwest Nebraska during the late afternoon on the 23rd, in response to an upper level disturbance approaching from the west. The thunderstorms tracked east, producing 64 mph winds in McCook.
episodes.213587: Clusters of strong thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon hours across central into north central Alabama. The storms produced gusty winds knocking down a few trees in Morgan County.
episodes.213614: Scattered thunderstorms occurred ahead of a frontal boundary on May 23-25. However, on May 25, a mesoscale convective system developed west of the area and enhanced the low level wind field.  This resulted in two tornadoes across the tri-state area. One tornado affected the Villa Tasso area in Walton county in Florida, and the other tornado affected Houston and Henry counties in Alabama.  Both tornadoes were rated EF1.
episodes.213627: Storms moved through SE Texas and produced strong winds and heavy rainfall.

episodes.213725: A cluster of strong to severe storms became organized as it progressed mostly across the I-20 corridor and surrounding areas in Louisiana. This thunderstorm activity produced numerous reports of wind damage as it was aided in its progression and intensity by an ongoing Mesoscale Convective Vortex (MCV).
episodes.213829: A mesoscale convective system developed from storms in south Texas and moved across the northwestern Gulf into coastal Louisiana.  This complex produced severe marine wind gusts, including a measured 81 mph gust near Cocodrie.
episodes.213830: A mesoscale convective system developed from storms in south Texas and moved across the northwestern Gulf into coastal Louisiana. As this complex reached the coastal waters south of Mississippi, severe marine wind gusts occurred.
episodes.213914: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. As a result, scattered severe thunderstorms developed during the late afternoon through the evening hours along the front, and produced multiple reports of large hail across Rusk and Panola Counties. While these storms diminished by mid-evening with the loss of heating/reduced instability, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana.
episodes.213916: A weak stationary front extended across East Texas and North Louisiana along the I-20 corridor during the afternoon hours of May 22nd, where a weak surface low drifted east along this boundary during the afternoon and evening. Meanwhile, weak upper level disturbances translated northeast atop this front in the southwest flow aloft, which both enhanced large scale forcing along the front within the moist and unstable air mass in place. An isolated severe thunderstorm developed during the early evening hours over the east side of Shreveport in Central Caddo Parish, producing quarter size hail in the Cedar Grove community before diminishing. While a lull in the storms were observed through the remainder of the evening into the overnight hours, a line of severe thunderstorms progressed east along the front into East Texas during the predawn hours of May 23rd, driven by a stronger upper level disturbance riding east along the front. Damaging winds and large hail accompanied these storms as they moved through much of Lower East Texas along/south of I-20 through the mid-morning hours, before exiting the area to the east into Western Louisiana. These storms eventually progressed east and exited Central Louisiana by midday on the 23rd.
episodes.213968: As the third week of May 2026 unfolded, the dynamic breakup front stalled repeatedly along the Lower Yukon, creating a cascading sequence of severe jams and flooding. This period involved massive downstream surges as well as backwater effects in tributaries like the Andreafsky and Chuilnuk.

episodes.214140: A unique event with limited severe weather and flash flooding occurred during the evening hours on May 22nd. A surface low pressure system slowly moved across western Kentucky, with a warm front extending to the east-northeast across much of Kentucky. Along and south of this warm front, precipitable water values exceeding 1.7 inches lead to showers and a few thunderstorms which produced efficient rainfall rates. Where heavier showers and storms trained over eastern Shelby, Henry, and western Franklin County, a few instances of flash flooding were observed. Closer to the surface low pressure center, marginal amounts of instability (around 250-500 J/kg MLCAPE) combined with relatively impressive amounts of low-level shear and helicity along the warm front to produce miniature supercells. One of these mini supercells produced a brief EF0 tornado in Butler County near Butler County High School.
episodes.214227: Scattered to numerous thunderstorms developed across southeast Georgia in the afternoon hours. One thunderstorm in Bulloch County became strong enough to produce hail.
episodes.214431: A tornadic supercell developed near or along the Kenedy/Kleberg County line during the evening of May 20, 2026. The storm tracked southeastward through Kenedy County before weakening just offshore Kenedy County that evening. A large hail and a very high wind gust (possible tornado) was reported as the supercell moved southeast and crossed Laguna Madre toward the nearshore Gulf waters.

The National Weather Service conducted a storm survey and determined that an EF0 85 mph tornado occurred in southwest Morgantown during the evening of Friday, May 22, 2026. ||Tree damage was first observed at a farm at the end of Viles Cemetery Road, where several treetops were damaged and pointing in different directions ranging from the southwest to southeast consistent with a convergent pattern from the small tornado. The damage continued to the east toward Viles Cemetery where some large branches were on the ground. Nearby Viles Cemetery Road, a field of tall grasses were bent and laying south in the direction of the tornado inflow.||The tornado continued across Gardner Lane where Final Finish Repair Shop sustained extensive roof damage. The roof was peeled back to the northwest direction, while a lot of insulation was carried eastward into nearby trees and power lines. Right to the |east of Final Finish Repair Shop, the tornado lifted with no additional ground damage. However, insulation from Final Finish Repair Shop was lofted into nearby fields, across the Natcher Parkway and in nearby trees at the Butler County High School Football Stadium. In total the short lived tornado was 0.32 miles long, although insulation from the Final Finish Repair Shop was observed at least another third of a mile from the end of the tornado as it was carried by the thunderstorm.

The Texas Coastal Oceanic Observation System platform at Rincon del San Jose, within Laguna Madre about one-third north of the Willacy/Kenedy County line, recorded a peak gust to 93 mph (80.86 knots) at 730 PM CDT.  This location is used as a proxy to the nearby land mass in Coastal Kenedy County, and based on the intensity of the supercell, it is certain that similar wind gusts occurred at this location. It is possible that the event produced a tornado - but lack of ground truth observations or a survey (in a very remote area accessible only by water craft) as well as the duration of the strong and shifting winds (nearly 20 minutes), as well as no sharply lowered surface pressure, suggest a rear-flank downburst as the strongest winds were from the north/northeast.

Gale force winds (34 knots or higher) arrived at approximately 721 PM, and soon reached Storm force (50.54 knots) at 724 PM.  Winds peaked at 80.86 knots at 730 PM and remained near storm force (46.65 knots) at 736 PM before finally dropping just below Gale force (33.24 knots) at 742 PM.  There was no known damage, including to the platform, as of this writing.

The NWS River Watch team observed severe, high-impact flooding at Pilot Station due to an ice jam. A river gauge registered a sudden 5-foot rise in a single day, eventually peaking at 33.76 feet on Sunday afternoon. All local roads became completely impassable except by boat, and multiple homes were impacted. Floodwaters officially exceeded 2024 levels, making this the worst flooding the community had seen since 1989.

The NWS River Watch team reported that heavy river ice jammed and backed up directly into the Andreafsky River near Saint Mary's, forcing it to flow backward upstream. Water levels rose significantly, causing damage to low-lying fish camps and smokehouses. Observers reported this as the highest water seen since the historic 1989 breakup.
